title: To live is Christ (Philippians 1:12–26)
hookLine: his chains have spread the news; to live is Christ, to die is gain

cards: Chains, and a guard who never leaves. In this letter Paul calls them his bonds, and he is plainly under guard. Every visitor is seen.
Every letter he dictates, someone overhears. Every prayer, too. Plenty of people would call that the end of their work.
Paul looks at the same situation and sees an audience. The friends at Philippi are worried about him, so he writes to tell them how it's actually going.

teach.h: THE PRISON HAS SPREAD THE NEWS.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel." The prison has helped, not hurt. "So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace."
Palace here is the praetorium, the Roman guard or the governor's headquarters.

The whole guard knows why he's chained, and other believers, seeing him unafraid, have grown bolder. Then something surprising. Some are preaching Christ out of rivalry, hoping to make his chains hurt more.

teach.h: RIVALS PREACH TOO, AND HE REJOICES.
teach.b: "What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice." He doesn't need to be the hero of the story.
Then the line in today's title: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." He's thinking out loud about his own trial. If he lives, he keeps working, which for him is Christ.
If he dies, he's with Christ, which he calls far better.
"I am in a strait betwixt two": hemmed in on both sides, pulled two ways. Then he chooses, as far as it's his choice: to stay is more needful for you.

teach.h: FOR TO ME TO LIVE IS CHRIST, AND TO DIE IS GAIN.
teach.b: He'll live for them. The passage is honest. It doesn't pretend death is nothing.
It says a life wrapped around something larger is a life even prison can't shrink.

how: Some Christians facing illness, prison or danger turn to Philippians 1:21, and it is sometimes read at Christian funerals.

o: the prison cell where Paul wrote his letters
the Roman court where Paul was finally tried
the Roman guard, or the governor's headquarters

games.q: what's inside Philippians 1:12–26 — tap the pairs.
p: preaching to add to his pain

s: Paul says his imprisonment has helped spread the gospel
"the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel."
Paul is angry at people who preach out of rivalry
"whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice."
in this passage Paul says death is nothing to him
he weighs it honestly, calls being with Christ far better, and chooses to stay for their sake.

games.q: you're in chains. you hear that some people are preaching just to make your situation worse. how do you respond?
o: rejoice that Christ is preached either way.
games.why: "What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice."

practice: Name one thing hemming you in right now, a job you can't leave yet, an illness, caring for a parent, money, a season of waiting, and look at it honestly without pretending it's good.
Then ask who is around you inside it that you wouldn't meet otherwise, and what you can do here that you couldn't anywhere else. If you pray, offer the constraint to God.

wordCard.voice: Praetorium. The Roman governor's headquarters where Paul's guard is stationed, so the whole guard knows why he's chained.

orig.note: Greek: to live, Christ. Paul's line is even shorter in Greek than in English.

carryVoice: Your line: a strait betwixt two. Pulled two ways, he chose the people who needed him. Another week on the path.
